rule: Ask about a recent concrete use/problem and existing alternatives before interpreting encouragement as demand.
Choose one channel with evidence that the intended audience is there, a native useful contribution, and an effort cap.
Connect alternatives, distinctive capability, user value and best-fit audience before writing the headline.
Tagged visits and attributed conversions do not prove incremental causal effects.
Do not sum platform reach into unique people without deduplicated identities and permission to use them.
reason: Repeated visitors and overlapping platform audiences violate distinct-person addition.

rule: Preserve raw metric definition, period, source and collection time; compare only compatible reporting scopes.
Describe captured reviewed reactions; do not label their sentiment distribution as market-wide opinion.
Keep lexical suggestions visibly unreviewed; read context, negation, sarcasm, language and identity before labeling.
Prespecify the audience, unit, allocation, outcome, duration, sample target and stop/review rule before interpreting a difference.
reason: A fixed-design confidence interval cannot correct uncontrolled sampling or repeated peeking.

rule: An observed starts/visitors ratio below 20% prompts a small usability investigation; it is not an industry benchmark or viability gate.
reason: House triage threshold; intended to direct attention, not judge success.

rule: Review separate evidence for problem/desire, activation, retained use and payment; do not collapse them into a popularity score.
Give each asset a clear next action and a tryable product that matches the audience's expectation.
Research direct alternatives, substitutes and the current way of doing the job, including doing nothing.
Define language, geography/payment access, platform, genre, constraint and price; require purchasing evidence and inadequate substitutes before calling a cohort underserved.
reason: House decision framework; market growth, wealth, preference and low language supply are separate proxies, not a validated opportunity score.

rule: Present each material demand claim with its primary source, publication/data/check dates, denominator, scope, credibility, relevance, counterevidence and inference status.
reason: House reporting contract; trusted sources can still have weak relevance to a specific paying cohort.

rule: Divide additional fixed delivery cost by net contribution per incremental retained sale; include QA and updates, regional realized receipts and buyers who would already buy English.
reason: Break-even arithmetic is not a sales forecast; a new-game decision must also include development cost.

rule: Match the next test to the project's stage: at idea, evidence that the problem or desire is real; at prototype, intended strangers reaching and finishing a first session; at beta, widening on the best-evidenced channel while the first session is fixed; at launched, a returning cohort, reviewed reception and a cadence the maker can sustain.
reason: House stage playbook built on the four-dimension discovery rubric (problem, activation, retention, payment). The stages are the owner's own labels and the order is a planning inference, not a published finding.

rule: Do not ask for activation or return evidence before something can be tried, and do not read a rate without its denominator: a return rate needs a cohort of starts, an activation ratio needs visitors and starts for the same window.
reason: A return rate is returns divided by starts for one cohort and window (craft/measurement.md). With nothing to try there are 0 starts, so the denominator is 0 and the rate is unknown, not zero.

rule: When several channels have a visitors-and-starts pair for the same window, take the next test to the one with the highest observed ratio and keep the others as comparisons; the ratio ranks what to try next and does not predict what more traffic would do.
reason: Observed ratios come from different audiences and unrandomized assignment (craft/experiments.md), and the counts may be different people, so they are descriptive.

rule: For a free game, test on a venue that costs nothing to enter (an itch.io page, a web portal's own test) before paying a store fee, and open a paid store page once first-session and return evidence exist.
reason: Entry costs on the cited pages: Steam $100 per product, not refundable and recouped only once the product has $1,000 adjusted gross revenue from the store and in-app purchases; Apple $99 a year; Google Play $25 once, and new personal accounts must also meet testing requirements before release. CrazyGames Basic Launch and Poki's tests cost nothing to enter. A free game with no in-app purchases has no adjusted gross revenue, so the Steam fee is not recouped from it. This is arithmetic on documented fees, not a forecast of what a store page earns.

rule: Open a store page only after its readiness gates pass: the name is settled, the page copy matches the pinned build, the store assets meet the store's current rules and the measurement works. Check recorded gates with marketing plan.
reason: Valve advises waiting to show a game until its art direction and core features are settled, reviews the page and the build against each other, and requires gameplay-only screenshots and only launch features; a new product's page must also be public for at least two weeks. Ordering the page behind its gates is a house planning rule, not a Valve requirement.

rule: Meet the store's written asset rules before review: on Steam, capsules at the exact pixel sizes carrying only game artwork, the game name and at most an official subtitle, and at least five gameplay-only screenshots of 1920x1080 or more at 16:9, on a page that lists only features available at launch.

Plan a Steam release from the longest wait Valve's pages state: the fee date plus 30 days (one page says 21), a public coming-soon page for at least two weeks, and a request for page and build review at least 7 business days before each go-live.
reason: The Steam Direct page states a 30-day wait before a first release and the Onboarding page 21. Tax verification is 2-7 business days in the Getting Started FAQ and 10 to 15 on Onboarding. Reviews are 1-5 days on two pages, and typically 3-5 business days with 7 business days of lead time on the Review Process page. Taking the longer figure of each pair cannot make a plan late by either page. The earliest release date is the latest of: fee date + 30 days, public coming-soon date + 14 days, and review request + 7 business days.

rule: Quote a trailer benchmark with its sample, median and n, and treat it as a description of trailers that exist, not of trailers that worked; Valve's own advice is that the first trailer be primarily gameplay.
reason: The first (page-lead) trailers of 27 comparable Steam pages have a median length of 67.8 s (quartiles 55.75 and 82.65 s, range 17.8 to 182.0 s, 18 of 27 over 60 s). The sample mixes launch, teaser, update and sales trailers, so it is not a launch-trailer benchmark, and nothing in it measures what a trailer did for wishlists.

rule: Record the query, the sort order and the date with any tag-based supply count, and re-run it under a second sort before quoting a denominator or a median.
reason: The same Farming Sim plus Space search returned 18 games sorted by Reviews_DESC (which drops games under 10 reviews), 30 sorted by Released_DESC and 60 by relevance (which includes unreleased pages). A first count of 33 Farming Sim plus Space-or-Sci-fi games with a median of 48 reviews became 53 released games with a median of 21 under a second sort.

rule: Answer each venue's AI disclosure from an inventory of what ships and how it was made: Steam asks about content that ships and is consumed by players (artwork, sound, narrative, localization) and holds the game to its marketing; itch.io asks for a tag per kind of content (graphics, sound, text and dialog, code); Newgrounds disallows games generated via an AI prompt and asks for disclosure in the author commentary.

Quote an AI-sentiment figure with the population that gave it: surveyed Steam players, surveyed core gamers and the reviews of games that disclosed measure different groups, and no source read measures cozy or casual players.

Decide the audience before choosing measurement: where children under 13 may play, a persistent identifier such as a cookie value, an IP address or a device ID is personal information under COPPA and marketing materials weigh in whether a service is child-directed, so add no identifier without asking counsel.

For a game with no analytics, read what each venue's own dashboard measures, record it under that venue's definition, tag the link where a venue reads tags, and never add one venue's counts to another's.
reason: A static host gives no visit counts (GitHub's documentation describes repository traffic, not visits to a Pages site), and a tagged query string survives in the address bar of a static game but nothing counts it unless the page or an analytics tool reads it (observed on one game, online and offline). The dashboards define views, plays and sessions differently (craft/measurement.md), so a sum would mix definitions.

rule: Search the name on the stores you plan to use, in the trademark register, and for domains and handles before paying a store fee or producing assets, and treat a same-name listing or a live registration as a decision for the owner and counsel. Marketing prior art is not legal clearance.
reason: The $100 Steam fee, the capsule art and the trailer are all spent against a name nobody has tested; a collision found afterwards means renaming the page, the assets and the trailer.

rule: Write each readiness gate as a check with a number taken from a documented limit or the project's own measurement; where no figure is known, record that it is an owner decision instead of inventing a threshold.
reason: A pair of wishlist bands in one dry-run plan (270 to continue, under 150 to stop within 14 days) had no source and borrowed a festival yield; an unsourced number reads like a benchmark and misleads more than an open owner decision.
